 After 32 years, Indiana Libertarians are just shy of the votes they need to keep ballot access
 Nearly 2 million Hoosiers voted in November. Turnout rose from about 40% in the last midterm to 42%, and nearly 45% of ballots were cast absentee.
 By 
 Casey Smith 
 - 
 November 19, 2026 5:00 am 
 Secretary of state was the top race for candidates this year in Indiana. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
 A few hundred votes could end the Indiana Libertarian Party’s 32-year run of automatic ballot access – and a new minor party has secured its place on future ballots.
 Libertarian Lauri Shillings received 38,663 votes in the race for Indiana secretary of state, or 1.987% of the 1,945,765 votes recorded in preliminary returns from all 92 counties.
 At that vote total, the 2% threshold is 38,916 votes, putting Shillings 253 short. Former Indianapolis Mayor Greg Ballard received 70,068 votes, or 3.60%, for the Lincoln Party.
 The final vote and turnout totals could still change slightly. County certified returns were due Tuesday, but counties have until Friday to make corrections, according to the Indiana Election Division.
 Stephanie Dasbach, chair of the Libertarian Party of Indiana, said the party is waiting for certified results and will help its 2028 candidates gather signatures if needed. She did not say whether the party would seek a recount or file a legal challenge if Shillings falls short however.
 “We cannot know anything until the final certified results are out,” Dasbach told the Indiana Capital Chronicle. “We will pursue any avenues we can to ensure that every vote is counted and that the election is secure.”
 The Nov. 3 election drew nearly 2 million Hoosiers, or about 42% of registered voters, up from about 40% in the 2022 midterms . The bigger change was in how people voted. Nearly 45% of ballots were cast absentee, up from about 37% four years earlier.
 Absentee in Indiana includes both in-person early voting and mail-in ballots.
 Laura Merrifield Wilson, a political science professor at the University of Indianapolis, said losing automatic ballot access would make it harder for Libertarians to field candidates under their party’s name.
 “Of course, if they’re able to clinch the 2%, then the conversation is moot,” Wilson said. “But that said, this would be I think a major loss for the party.”
 What 2% gets a party
 Democrat Beau Bayh won the secretary of state race with 1,007,815 votes, or 51.8%, in the preliminary count. Republican Max Engling received 829,083 votes, or 42.6%.
 For the two minor parties, the same race determined how easily they could put candidates on the ballot in future elections.
 Indiana allows a minor party whose secretary of state candidate receives at least 2% and less than 10% of the vote to nominate candidates by convention. If the preliminary results hold, the Lincoln Party would gain that option and the Libertarians would lose it.
 Libertarian candidates seeking a printed spot on the ballot will have to petition for it. The signature requirement is based on 2% of the vote in the most recent secretary of state race within the district the candidate seeks to represent.
 Libertarian candidate Lauri Shillings listens to a question during the Indiana Secretary of State Debate hosted by the Indiana Debate Commission, Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, at WFYI Public Television Studios in Indianapolis. (Photo by Doug McSchooler for Indiana Debate Commission) 
 The Libertarian Party of Indiana has held ballot access since 1994.
 Dasbach said the party expected Shillings to clear 2%. She said Shillings was “largely locked out of the media coverage given to her three opponents” and still drew more than 38,000 votes.
 “The results of this election showed that a significant Hoosiers continue to want more options and are dissatisfied with what the Republicans and Democrats are sending them. Nearly 6% of Hoosiers voiced their displeasure with the major party candidates in a very high-profile, high-turnout race in which candidates spent millions of dollars,” Dasbach said. “Obviously, our expectations were to reach the 2% ballot threshold, but this was a uniquely challenging race and environment this season.”
 The next secretary of state race in 2030 would give the party another chance to qualify for automatic ballot access.
 Dasbach said the party expects to change how it recruits and supports candidates and members regardless of the final tally.
 Wilson pointed to a competitive race between the major-party nominees and a second option for voters looking beyond those parties as two factors that may have made it harder for Shillings to reach 2%.
 She said Ballard, a former Republican, may have appealed to moderate Republicans who wanted an alternative to their party’s nominee.
 Losing automatic access could change where Libertarians put their time and resources ahead of the next election, Wilson said.
 Voters make their selections at Allisonville Christian Church in Indianapolis on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle) 
 “Now they’re going to have to look at candidate recruitment probably a little bit differently, at the political infrastructure for campaigns a little differently,” Wilson added. “I think they were likely able to rely on a base of libertarian or nonpartisan voters who chose them because they were an alternative to the two primary parties, not necessarily because of what they stood for or that those voters were super loyal or allegiant to the libertarian message.”
 About one in three of Ballard’s votes came from Marion and Hamilton counties, which together accounted for about one in five votes in the secretary of state race. Ballard drew 5.9% in Marion County and 5.3% in Hamilton County, compared with 3.6% statewide.
 Shillings received at least 2% of the secretary of state vote in 62 of Indiana’s 92 counties, according to preliminary precinct returns.
 Chad Kinsella, an associate professor of political science at Ball State University, said it’s hard to know how voters would have voted in a race without Ballard.
 “Some of those people could have gone to the Lincoln Party, but I don’t know that if we got rid of the Lincoln Party, that all of those people or even some of those people would have necessarily gone to Libertarians,” he said. “I think there’s a group of people out there that are disaffected. And I have a feeling that this election, it was a lot of Republicans that were very happy to go for any third party because they were really angry with their party.”
 More absentee ballots, fewer Election Day votes
 Indiana recorded 1,997,142 ballots from 4,768,979 registered voters in this year’s preliminary turnout figures. That’s 115,582 more ballots than in 2022, when 1,881,560 Hoosiers voted. Turnout rose from 39.5% to 41.9%.
 The state recorded 892,609 absentee ballots this year, nearly 204,000 more than the 2022 report listed. The reported Election Day count fell from about 1.2 million four years ago to about 1.1 million this year. Indiana’s absentee category includes early in-person voting and voting by mail.
 Indiana recorded nearly 204,000 more absentee ballots than the state reported in 2022, even though the overall number of ballots grew by only 116,000. The reported Election Day count fell by about 94,000.
 Bayh puts Indiana Democrats back in winning column with secretary of state victory 
 In Tippecanoe County, about 38% of registered voters cast a ballot, up from 32% in 2022. The county’s absentee share rose from about 47% to 60%.
 Marion County recorded nearly 38,000 more ballots than in 2022, with turnout rising from 34% to 41%. Hamilton County turnout increased from 48% to 52%, and its absentee share climbed from 41% to 53%. In Monroe County, turnout jumped from 41% to 47%.
 In Johnson County, turnout held at about 39%, but the share of ballots cast absentee rose from 47% in 2022 to 55% this year.
 Still, overall turnout remained below Indiana’s last two presidential elections.
 State turnout figures show that about 65% of registered voters cast ballots in 2020 and 62% did so in 2024.
 Wilson said competitive races can give voters more reason to participate. She also said some of the growth in absentee voting likely reflects people who would have voted on Election Day taking advantage of an earlier opportunity.
 “To see increases in terms of early voting and absentee voting certainly speaks to voter enthusiasm,” Wilson said. “I think it speaks to voter engagement.”
 Kinsella said the shift in how Hoosiers cast their ballots stood out more than the rise in turnout. He expects more voters to take advantage of absentee options over time.
 “I think here, election day voting is still going to be big,” he said. “But I do expect there are going to be more people that are going to be taking advantage of those options for voting absentee.”

 Author Info
 Casey Smith
 A lifelong Hoosier, Casey Smith previously reported on the Indiana Legislature for The Associated Press. She holds a master’s degree in investigative reporting and narrative writing from the University of California/Berkeley’s Graduate School of Journalism. She previously earned degrees in journalism, anthropology and Spanish from Ball State University, where she now serves as an instructor of journalism. 
Her reporting has earned the Goldsmith Prize for Investigative Reporting, the George Polk Award, the Selden Ring Award, and recognition as a Pulitzer Prize finalist, among other honors. Smith was named Indiana Journalist of the Year by the Society of Professional Journalists' Indiana Chapter in May 2025 for her in-depth reporting on state government, law enforcement and the death penalty.
